meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is absurd'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Voltaire: an 1770 letter to Prince Frederick William of Prussia, attacking d’Holbach. Here’s the source, the French original, and the full line.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: From Voltaire’s letter of 28 November 1770 to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia. The wording most people quote is S. G. Tallentyre’s 1919 English translation in Voltaire in His Letters ↗; the French original reads ‘l’assurance est un état ridicule.’

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Letter to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia

source.excerpt: Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is an absurd one. What is most repellent in the System of Nature — after the recipe for making eels from flour — is the audacity with which it decides that there is no God, without even having tried to prove the impossibility.
trail: The line comes from Voltaire’s letter of 28 November 1770 to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia, catalogued in the sourced section of Wikiquote ↗ — not among its misattributed or disputed entries.
WIST ↗ pins the English wording to S. G. Tallentyre’s 1919 translation, Voltaire in His Letters, and prints the French original alongside it.
QuotePark ↗ preserves the fuller sentence, where Voltaire goes on to mock d’Holbach’s Système de la nature for declaring there is no God without proving it.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version keeps only the first clause — and drops the jab at d’Holbach that follows
source.excerptNote: In the original French: ‘Le doute n’est pas un état bien agréable, mais l’assurance est un état ridicule.’ Tallentyre’s choice of ‘certainty…absurd’ is the wording that went viral; other translations give ‘ridiculous’ for ridicule, and some paraphrases open with ‘Uncertainty is an uncomfortable position.’ All render the same genuine sentence.

author.name: Voltaire
author.heading: About Voltaire
author.bio: Voltaire — pen name of François-Marie Arouet — was the wit and conscience of the French Enlightenment, a prolific author of plays, histories, essays and some fifteen thousand surviving letters. A lifelong deist, he championed religious tolerance and free inquiry while attacking dogmatism of every stripe. This line comes from that skeptical temperament: written in old age, it rebukes the confident atheism of d’Holbach as just another kind of certainty he distrusted.

context.heading: Why it matters
lead: Voltaire wrote this in his mid-seventies, at Ferney, as Europe’s philosophes split over Baron d’Holbach’s anonymously published Système de la nature (1770) — a thoroughgoing atheist, materialist manifesto. A deist to the end, Voltaire found its dogmatic certainty as objectionable as the religious dogmatism he had spent a lifetime fighting.

The famous first clause is the hinge of that critique: doubt is uncomfortable, he concedes, but the person who claims to have settled the biggest questions for good has simply traded one absurdity for another. It is skepticism turned against the confident unbelievers as readily as the believers.
context.detailsSummary: A note on the recipient and the wandering wording
detailsBody: The letter is addressed to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia (1744–1797), nephew and heir of Frederick the Great — not to Frederick II himself, though some compilations blur the two. It is occasionally mis-dated to 1767, conflating it with an earlier letter to the King.

Because the quote survives mainly through translation, its English form drifts: ‘an absurd one,’ ‘a ridiculous one,’ and the looser ‘Uncertainty is an uncomfortable position…’ all circulate. They are variant renderings of one authentic sentence, not separate quotations.
context.pull: Doubt is uncomfortable — but the person who is certain has only traded one absurdity for another.
